title: Tomorrow, and making plans
goal: Talk about the future — again with no future tense — invite someone, accept, decline gracefully, and use *kalau* to say what you will do if something happens.
bekal: invite, accept and refuse an invitation the Indonesian way
say what might happen with *mungkin*, *kalau* and *semoga*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Diajak ke Bandung
dialogs.intro: Thursday afternoon. Rina has an idea for the weekend.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Sarah, akhir pekan ini ada rencana?
lines.id: Sarah, do you have plans this weekend?
lines.literal: Sarah, end week this exist plan?

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Kami mau ke Bandung. Mau ikut?
lines.id: We're going to Bandung. Do you want to come?
lines.literal: we want to Bandung. want follow?

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Sabtu pagi. Nanti kita naik travel.
lines.id: Saturday morning. We'll take a shared minivan.
lines.literal: Saturday morning. later we ride travel.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Minggu sore. Kalau macet, mungkin malam.

lines.literal: Sunday afternoon. if jammed, maybe night.

lines.text: Di rumah tante saya. Tenang, tidak usah bayar.

lines.text: Nggak usah repot. Tapi boleh juga, hehe.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Oke, sampai Sabtu. Semoga tidak hujan!
lines.id: OK, see you Saturday. Let's hope it doesn't rain!
lines.literal: OK, until Saturday. hopefully not rain!

notes: **Mau ikut? — the standard invitation.** *Ikut* means "to come along, to join, to follow", and it is one of the most useful verbs in Indonesian social life. *Saya ikut* = "I'm in". *Boleh ikut?* = "can I come too?"

**Nothing in this dialogue marks the future except the situation.** *Berangkat Sabtu pagi*, *kita naik travel*, *kita menginap* — all bare verbs. Because *akhir pekan ini* has set the frame, no *akan* is needed anywhere. Adding it would not be wrong, just heavier.
**Tidak usah — "no need".** It is softer than *tidak boleh* and warmer than *tidak perlu*, and it is the standard way to wave away an offer or a worry. 💬 In speech: *nggak usah*.

**Travel** is a genuine Indonesian word — a shared door-to-door minivan service between cities, booked by phone or app. It is pronounced roughly *TRÉ-vel*, and it will not be in your dictionary with that meaning.

**Semoga — "may it be that…", "hopefully".** It opens every good wish in the language: *Semoga sukses* (good luck), *Semoga cepat sembuh* (get well soon), *Semoga selamat sampai tujuan* (safe travels). It is warm, common and completely regular.

grammars.title: Talking about what is to come
body: Four words, in rough order from most certain to least.
after: *Rencana* is "a plan", and *rencananya* — with the *-nya* you now know well — means "the plan is". *Rencananya kami berangkat Sabtu* is exactly how an Indonesian would open a description of a trip.

⚠️ Be careful with *mau*. Because it means both "want to" and "about to", *Saya mau pergi* can be a wish or an announcement. The context always sorts it out, but when you truly mean desire and it matters, use *ingin*.

grammars.title: Kalau — the conditional you already have
body: Indonesian has no conditional verb forms. It has *kalau*, and that is the entire system.

head: Indonesian
Word for word
English
rows: If it rains, we'll stay in.
I'll call if I get a chance.

after: *Kalau tidak salah* — "if I'm not mistaken" — is worth memorising as a block. It is the Indonesian way of stating something you are only fairly sure of, and it appears in conversation constantly.
For hypothetical, contrary-to-fact conditions you would need *seandainya* or *kalau saja*. That is B1 work; at A1, *kalau* handles everything.

head: Indonesian
English
Note
rows: Not sure yet, I'll let you know.
I'll come if I get the chance.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Read the maybes carefully.** *Belum tentu*, *lain kali*, *nanti saya kabari*, *kalau sempat* — from an Indonesian these are usually a gentle no. Nobody is being evasive to annoy you; refusing outright feels harsh, so the language provides a set of soft exits. Use them yourself and you will fit right in.
The verb *kabari* ("let someone know") is built from *kabar*, the news word you met on day one in *Apa kabar?*. *Nanti saya kabari* is one of the most useful sentences in Indonesian working life.

head: Indonesian
English
When
rows: Have a good day at work.
Give my regards to the family.

blocks.text: *Selamat* again — the same "safe" word that opened Unit 1. Indonesian builds almost every congratulation and good wish out of it, so if you can hear *selamat* plus a verb, you can decode most of them: *selamat datang* (welcome), *selamat makan*, *selamat belajar*, *selamat tidur*.

*Titip salam* is lovely and untranslatable: *titip* means "to entrust something to someone" and *salam* is a greeting. You are entrusting your greeting to the person in front of you, for delivery. Say it when someone is going home to family, and watch them smile.
